questions.q: What are MongoDB's three levels of data organization, in order?
options: Database, collection, document
Server, table, row
Cluster, shard, partition
Instance, schema, object
questions.explain: A database hosts collections, and a collection groups documents — MongoDB's real three-level hierarchy.

questions.q: What is the one structural detail missing from saying 'a collection is just a table with a different name'?
options: A collection doesn't enforce that every document share the same fields, types, or constraints the way a relational table's schema does
Collections can't hold more than one document
Collections are physically stored differently on disk than tables, with no other difference
Collections require a primary key while tables don't
questions.explain: The key structural difference is that MongoDB doesn't enforce a shared schema across documents in a collection by default, unlike a relational table.

questions.q: What does 'schema-less by default' actually mean, per this lesson?
options: MongoDB doesn't enforce a schema at the engine level unless you opt in, but real applications still have an implicit schema and MongoDB supports optional schema validation
MongoDB documents literally have no structure of any kind, ever
MongoDB requires every document to be schema-validated before insertion
Schema-less means MongoDB cannot store structured data
questions.explain: The 'by default' qualifier matters — flexibility is the default, but enforcement (schema validation) is available when a team chooses it.

questions.q: What is the practical consequence for a DBA moving from SQL Server to MongoDB, regarding data integrity, per this lesson?
options: The engine no longer catches a malformed record the way a NOT NULL constraint or foreign key would — integrity becomes more of an application/validation-layer responsibility by default
MongoDB enforces stricter data integrity than SQL Server by default
There is no difference in how data integrity is handled between the two platforms
MongoDB makes foreign keys mandatory on every collection
questions.explain: Without schema validation explicitly configured, MongoDB doesn't provide the same engine-level integrity guarantees a relational table's constraints do.

questions.q: Why does this lesson frame MongoDB's flexible document model as a deliberate architectural bet rather than a missing feature?
options: It's a real tradeoff: matching the application's evolving data shape without a blocking schema migration on every change, at the cost of engine-enforced structure
MongoDB's developers simply forgot to implement schema enforcement
There is no real tradeoff — flexibility has no downside
Schema enforcement was removed from MongoDB in a recent version
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly ties this back to Lesson 1's framing: it's a deliberate bet on matching real, evolving application data shapes, not carelessness.
